reason: The sources provide 15 distinct claims supported across multiple independent sites detailing Mariner 4's historical flyby, hand-drawn first image, and surprising micrometeoroid encounter.
story: In 1964, humanity set out to solve the ancient mystery of Mars. After Mariner 3 failed when its payload shroud jammed, Mariner 4 launched with a new metal fairing. On July 14–15, 1965, Mariner 4 made history as the first probe to fly by Mars, passing just 6,118 miles above the surface. Anxious JPL engineers couldn't wait hours for computer image processing, so they hand-colored a raw numerical pixel printout using art pastels. The resulting images shocked the world: instead of alien cities or lush canals, Mars was a dead, moon-like world covered in ancient craters. Mariner 4 also measured a paper-thin atmosphere and icy daytime temperatures of minus 148 degrees Fahrenheit. Two years later, while cruising silently through deep space, Mariner 4 was sandblasted by a surprise meteoroid storm—likely debris from a shattered, lost comet.
angle: Before computers could process the first close-up photo of Mars, impatient NASA engineers created it by hand-coloring a numerical pixel printout with pastels.

claims.claim: Mariner 3 failed on launch day when its protective payload shroud failed to jettison.
Mariner 4 launched in November 1964 equipped with a redesigned all-metal payload fairing.
Mariner 4 became the first spacecraft to successfully fly by Mars and return close-up images of another planet from deep space.
Mariner 4 reached its closest approach to Mars on July 14–15, 1965, passing about 6,118 miles (9,846 kilometers) above the surface.
Mariner 4 carried a spare magnetic tape recorder that was not originally intended for its flight mission.
JPL team members hand-colored a numerical ticker-tape printout of pixel data using pastels to verify the camera worked before computers finished processing the image.
Mariner 4's close-up photographs revealed Mars to be a dead, heavily cratered Moon-like world, quashing long-held beliefs in canals and Martian civilizations.
Mariner 4 measured a thin Martian atmospheric pressure between 4 and 7 millibars.
Mariner 4 recorded daytime surface temperatures on Mars of minus 100 degrees Celsius (minus 148 degrees Fahrenheit).
Mariner 4 detected no magnetic field surrounding Mars.
On September 15, 1967, Mariner 4 unexpectedly encountered a severe micrometeoroid shower while cruising in space.
Scientists proposed that the 1967 meteoroid shower resulted from Mariner 4 passing near debris of the lost comet D/1895 Q1 (Swift).
Mariner 4 used the star Canopus as a navigational reference object for attitude star tracking.
Mariner 4 communicated with Earth tracking stations located in Goldstone (California), South Africa, and Australia.
Mariner 4 reduced its scientific data transmission rate from 33 1/3 bits per second to 8 1/3 bits per second during its interplanetary cruise.

disputed: Final termination date of contact: S1 and S6 state communications were terminated on December 21, 1967, whereas S2 states contact was maintained until December 31, 1967. A script should attribute or state 'late December 1967'.

Pastel color choices on the hand-colored image: S4 notes the creator bought pastels for a greyscale gradient without intentionally picking Martian red colors, while S1 simply describes a pastel set used paint-by-numbers style. Attribute individual artistic choices to Richard Grumm's account.
